content: 1. As new prevention methods and delivery systems are introduced, it is essential to adapt monitoring systems to collect and utilize individual-level data effectively for HIV prevention. 2. A system for unique identification is necessary to track individuals within and across services, ensuring data deduplication. 3. Mechanisms should be in place to identify individuals and priority populations who could benefit from HIV prevention interventions. 4. Health information systems must maintain confidentiality and anonymity to protect sensitive data. 5. Standardized tools and processes for data collection are critical to ensure consistency and reliability. 6. A minimum dataset of essential elements should be collected to monitor HIV prevention efforts effectively. 7. Maintaining confidentiality of individual-level health information is particularly important for populations at risk of criminalization, stigma, and discrimination, such as key populations and adolescents. 8. In many settings, behaviors like same-gender sexual activity, sex work, or drug use are stigmatized or criminalized, which can discourage individuals from accessing health services. 9. Health services collecting personally identifiable information linked to these behaviors may expose individuals to potential legal or social consequences, such as questioning, detention, or arrest by law enforcement. 10. Awareness that such information is being recorded may lead to underreporting of risk behaviors or avoidance of health services altogether. 11. Discrimination by healthcare workers based on behavior or identity, including denial of services, is a significant concern. 12. Healthcare workers play a central role in ensuring confidentiality and must be trained on the sensitivity of data, stigma, discrimination, and the importance of data protection. 13. Supervisors should include adherence to confidentiality procedures as a key component of personnel evaluations. 14. Staff with access to sensitive data may be required to sign confidentiality agreements, and national legislation for personal data protection should be in place and adhered to. 15. To minimize risks associated with collecting sensitive information, it is advisable not to use names, national ID numbers, or other personally identifying information in data systems. 16. Sensitive behavioral information should not be linked to personally identifiable information in HIV prevention data systems. 17. When linking HIV prevention data systems to other clinical datasets, such as those for HIV treatment, sensitive behavioral information should remain separate from personal identifiers. 18. For data analysis, reporting, and aggregation outside clinical service provision, all individual-level data should be de-identified or anonymized. 19. Anonymous unique identification (UID) codes allow for effective service provision and longitudinal tracking without collecting personally identifiable information. 20. UID codes should be assigned at the first point of engagement with the data system and used consistently across services and programs. 21. UID codes can be composed of information easily recalled by clients, enabling reconstruction when accessing services. 22. Consistent use of the same UID codes across services and programs is ideal for tracking individuals effectively. 23. Comprehensive health information systems to implement UIDs may take time to establish, but using individual-level prevention data at local levels can still improve data accuracy and reliability for monitoring and planning. 24. HIV prevention programs must understand the vulnerabilities, risks, values, and preferences of the individuals and communities they serve. 25. Social attitudes, such as those based on age, gender, ethnicity, disability, and criminalization of key populations, can increase HIV acquisition risk and limit access to prevention interventions. 26. Individual and partner behaviors, such as sexual activity, drug use, and viral suppression status, are critical determinants of HIV risk. 27. Risk levels can change over time due to changes in behavior, partnerships, or partner viral suppression status. 28. HIV prevalence and incidence in the surrounding geographic area also influence individual risk. 29. Combining population-level data on HIV prevalence/incidence with individual-level risk differentiation can help prioritize prevention services. 30. National HIV programs should review epidemiological data to identify subpopulations with higher HIV incidence/prevalence for prioritized prevention services. 31. Globally, key populations such as men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, transgender individuals, and people in prisons are disproportionately affected by HIV. 32. Some individuals may have overlapping vulnerabilities, such as sex workers who also inject drugs, increasing their risk of HIV acquisition. 33. Adolescent girls, young women, and serodiscordant couples with unsuppressed viral loads are also at substantial risk, particularly in southern and eastern Africa. 34. Not all individuals within these groups are at high risk at all times, and identifying those who may benefit from prevention services can be challenging. 35. Prioritizing prevention services and monitoring systems for populations at substantial risk can enable more efficient follow-up for those testing HIV-negative. 36. Differentiating individuals at substantial risk of HIV can be built into health information systems to aid providers in offering appropriate services and follow-up. 37. Conversations between service providers and clients are key to understanding individual HIV prevention needs and may occur before or after testing or during sexual health consultations. 38. Discussing stigmatized or criminalized behaviors, such as sexual activity or drug use, can be uncomfortable for both clients and providers, emphasizing the need for privacy and confidentiality. 39. Community-led services and peer workers play an important role in creating trusted and safe environments for these conversations. 40. Providers should offer prevention interventions to all individuals requesting them, even if they are unwilling to discuss their reasons for concern. 41. Some individuals may not recognize their own vulnerability to HIV, particularly adolescents and young adults, even when they have known risk factors like recent STIs. 42. Prevention prioritization tools, such as risk assessment questionnaires, can help individuals unaware of their risk or uncomfortable discussing it with healthcare workers to start conversations about HIV prevention. 43. Health information systems can record answers to these questions to guide prevention efforts. 44. Prevention prioritization tools have been validated for different populations, such as men who have sex with men in the USA, pregnant women in eastern Africa, and adolescent girls in South Africa. 45. A recent study in Zimbabwe found that a nine-question tool identified 77% of adolescent girls and young women who acquired HIV or HSV-2 within 12 months. 46. While these tools can identify individuals at higher risk, they should not be used to exclude access to prevention services for those requesting them. 47. Risk can change rapidly, and frequent data collection is necessary to ensure relevance. 48. In high-prevalence settings, questions on risk factors can help prioritize prevention services and prompt regular follow-up for individuals who may not recognize their own risk. 49. Questions may also be self-administered, allowing individuals to assess their own risk and motivate protective actions. 50. Prevention prioritization tools should not be used to exclude individuals from HIV prevention interventions, especially if they have self-identified as needing services.
